{{short description|Square matrix whose entries are 1 along the anti-diagonal and 0 elsewhere}}

In [[mathematics]], especially [[linear algebra]], the '''exchange matrices''' (also called the '''reversal matrix''', '''backward identity''', or '''standard involutory permutation''') are special cases of [[permutation matrix|permutation matrices]], where the 1 elements reside on the [[Main_diagonal#Antidiagonal|antidiagonal]] and all other elements are zero. In other words, they are 'row-reversed' or 'column-reversed' versions of the [[identity matrix]].<ref>{{citation|title=Matrix Analysis|first1=Roger A.|last1=Horn|first2=Charles R.|last2=Johnson|edition=2nd|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2012|isbn=978-1-139-78888-5 |chapter=§0.9.5.1 n-by-n reversal matrix |page=33|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O7sgAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA33}}.</ref>

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  J_2 &= \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & 1 \\
    1 & 0
  \end{pmatrix} \\[4pt]
  J_3 &= \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & 0 & 1 \\
    0 & 1 & 0 \\
    1 & 0 & 0
  \end{pmatrix} \\
  &\quad \vdots \\[2pt]
  J_n &= \begin{pmatrix}
    0      & 0      & \cdots      & 0      & 1      \\
    0      & 0      & \cdots      & 1      & 0      \\
    \vdots & \vdots & \,{}_{_{\displaystyle\cdot}} \!\, {}^{_{_{\displaystyle\cdot}}} \! \dot\phantom{j} & \vdots & \vdots \\ 
    0      & 1      & \cdots      & 0      & 0      \\
    1      & 0      & \cdots      & 0      & 0      
  \end{pmatrix}
\end{align}</math><!-- there is no diagonal dots symbol in the antidiagonal direction so a bit of creativity was needed -->

==Definition==
If {{mvar|J}} is an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} exchange matrix, then the elements of {{mvar|J}} are
<math display="block">J_{i,j} = \begin{cases} 
1, & i + j = n + 1 \\
0, & i + j \ne n + 1\\
\end{cases}</math>

==Properties==
* Premultiplying a matrix by an exchange matrix flips vertically the positions of the former's rows, i.e.,<math display=block>
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix}
7 & 8 & 9 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
1 & 2 & 3
\end{pmatrix}.
</math>
* Postmultiplying a matrix by an exchange matrix flips horizontally the positions of the former's columns, i.e.,<math display=block>
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix}
3 & 2 & 1 \\
6 & 5 & 4 \\
9 & 8 & 7
\end{pmatrix}.
</math>
* Exchange matrices are [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]]; that is: <math display=block>
  J_n^\mathsf{T} = J_n.</math>
* For any [[integer]] {{mvar|k}}: <math display=block>
  J_n^k = \begin{cases}
  I & \text{ if } k \text{ is even,} \\[2pt]
  J_n & \text{ if } k \text{ is odd.}
  \end{cases}
  </math>In particular, {{mvar|J<sub>n</sub>}} is an [[involutory matrix]]; that is, <math display=block>
  J_n^{-1} = J_n.</math>
* The [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of {{mvar|J<sub>n</sub>}} is 1 if {{mvar|n}} is odd and 0 if {{mvar|n}} is even. In other words: <math display=block>
  \operatorname{tr}(J_n) = \frac{1-(-1)^n}{2} = n\bmod 2.</math>
* The [[determinant]] of {{mvar|J<sub>n</sub>}} is: <math display=block>
  \det(J_n) = (-1)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} = (-1)^\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
  </math> As a function of {{mvar|n}}, it has period 4, giving 1, 1, −1, −1 when {{mvar|n}} is [[modular arithmetic|congruent modulo 4]] to 0, 1, 2, and 3 respectively.
* The [[characteristic polynomial]] of {{mvar|J<sub>n</sub>}} is: <math display=block>
  \det(\lambda I- J_n) = (\lambda -1)^{\lceil n/2\rceil}(\lambda +1)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}=
\begin{cases}
  \big[(\lambda+1)(\lambda-1)\big]^\frac{n}{2} & \text{ if } n \text{ is even,} \\[4pt]
  (\lambda-1)^\frac{n+1}{2}(\lambda+1)^\frac{n-1}{2} & \text{ if } n \text{ is odd,}
  \end{cases}</math>
its [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] are 1 (with multiplicity <math>\lceil n/2\rceil</math>) and -1 (with multiplicity <math>\lfloor n/2\rfloor</math>).
* The [[adjugate matrix]] of {{mvar|J<sub>n</sub>}} is: <math display=block>
  \operatorname{adj}(J_n) = \sgn(\pi_n)  J_n.
  </math> (where {{math|sgn}} is the [[Parity of a permutation|sign]] of the [[permutation]] {{mvar|&pi;{{sub|k}}}} of {{mvar|k}} elements).

==Relationships==
* An exchange matrix is the simplest [[anti-diagonal matrix]].
* Any matrix {{mvar|A}} satisfying the condition {{math|1=''AJ'' = ''JA''}} is said to be [[centrosymmetric matrix|centrosymmetric]].
* Any matrix {{mvar|A}} satisfying the condition {{math|1=''AJ = JA''<sup>T</sup>}} is said to be [[persymmetric matrix|persymmetric]].
* Symmetric matrices {{mvar|A}} that satisfy the condition {{math|1=''AJ = JA''}} are called [[Bisymmetric matrix|bisymmetric]] matrices. Bisymmetric matrices are both centrosymmetric and persymmetric.

==See also==
* [[Pauli matrices]] (the first Pauli matrix is a 2 × 2 exchange matrix)
